summary:
Travellers to Hauts-de-France stand under France's national framework: criminal law, identity-document rules, anti-discrimination law and marriage law apply uniformly across the region, and the country's oversight bodies record the same pattern of risk everywhere. The risks documented for transgender travellers in France concentrate in two settings: detention and the border. In everyday movement, accommodation and services, oversight bodies record persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition.

Prison placement follows no statutory rule. Under Article D248 of the criminal-procedure code men and women must be held in separate establishments, but placement follows the legal gender inscribed on identity documents, so trans women still recorded as male are held in all-male facilities. Controller-general Adeline Hazan, the national detention inspector-general, identifies transgender detainees as the group that suffers the most in prison. Each facility improvises: special units, or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates.

The BuzzFeed News investigation of 12 January 2018 documents that practice in the region directly. Paola, transferred in 2014 to Lille's northern correctional facility, was met by detainees shouting that they did not want any women there, was attacked by a fellow inmate with a knife, and spent two days in solitary confinement. Kara B. was held under conditions described as worrying after her 2016 Paris protest trial. The Ministry of Justice counted 13 transgender detainees across eight facilities as of 1 November 2016. Accounts collected in the same feature describe heightened assault vulnerability and suicide risk under isolation arrangements.

France's national custodial-inspection authority, the CGLPL, examined roughly 40 referrals from trans detainees since 2010 and issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 covering every place of deprivation of liberty. It finds that assignment to establishments or wards is based exclusively on civil status, so the vast majority of transgender people are held in institutions or wards that do not correspond to their gender identity, and that search procedures for persons whose civil-status sex does not match their identity add constraints such as isolation. The opinion records no marked improvement since its 2010 opinion despite the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform, and its findings rest on a decade of letters from detained trans people.

The CGLPL opinion recommends guaranteeing every transgender detainee the possibility of choosing the sex of searching officers and of their ward, bars identity-based isolation, requires continuity of medical and hormone care with free choice of doctor, and urges research funding. It faults the administration for not translating the 2016 justice-modernisation law (n° 2016-1547 of 18 November 2016) into prison rules, and issues binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty. Its scope now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at the airport, questioned in front of other travellers, documenting identity-document friction for trans travellers arriving in France.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights, confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition, the legal baseline dates from the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.
tangentialFactors:
Placement practice has drawn sustained political attention. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October; her incarceration was raised before the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, arguing that the case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees.

The national preventive mechanism told the Association for the Prevention of Torture that a new opinion was needed precisely because the 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement, because the gender-recognition law and its terminology had changed, and because coverage now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees. Structural problems were identified in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention.

The European comparison point is the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, which places France at 64% for identity-related discrimination reported by trans people, a figure the Défenseur des droits uses to anchor its guidance to service providers.

Regional detention exposure is quantifiable rather than hypothetical: the Ministry of Justice count of 13 transgender detainees in eight facilities as of 1 November 2016, together with roughly 40 referrals received by the custodial-inspection authority since 2010.
localsOnly:
Residents held in the region's establishments are assigned by civil status alone. Article D248 of the criminal-procedure code separates men and women into different establishments, and no statutory rule governs placement of transgender prisoners, so facilities decide individually between special units and isolation.

The CGLPL opinion of 25 May 2021 sets out binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty: every transgender detainee must be able to choose the sex of searching officers and their ward, identity-based isolation is barred, medical and hormone care must continue without interruption with free choice of doctor, and research funding is urged.

The administration is faulted for not translating the 2016 justice-modernisation law (n° 2016-1547 of 18 November 2016) into prison rules; that gap is why practice has not improved since the 2010 opinion, and coverage now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees.

Complaint and guidance machinery for residents runs through the Défenseur des droits, whose framework decision on trans rights draws on case files and association testimony and instructs service providers. Anti-discrimination claims in services and accommodation sit under the same national framework.

Partner recognition rests on the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the CGLPL's 2021 recommendations have been implemented in Hauts-de-France's establishments is unresolved: the inventory sources the recommendations and the finding of no marked improvement since 2010, but not post-2021 compliance data for this region.

No sourced figure exists in the inventory for transgender detainees held in Hauts-de-France facilities specifically; the only custodial count available is the national Ministry of Justice figure of 13 detainees in eight facilities as of 1 November 2016.

Border-document friction is documented for French airports through a single first-person account of 7 March 2017; practice at Hauts-de-France entry points, including regional airports and the Channel and Belgian crossings, is not sourced here.

Hate-crime charging and conviction outcomes for offences against transgender people in the region are not covered by these sources.
